clue.text: Excelled protecting one note well: it may be hacked

indicators.note: to protect something is to wrap round it, so one piece goes around the others

blocks.note: to shine at something is to excel; past tense
the Roman numeral for one
nota bene, Latin for note well

explanation.surface: A star performer guards a single note in a hacking scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: SH(I NB)ONE. In football, hacking is kicking an opponent's shins, so the bone at the front of the lower leg is what gets hacked.
explanation.definitionFit: Hacking in football means kicking an opponent's lower leg, so the front leg bone is a cryptic example of a hacked target.

clue.text: Charge covering mass swindle

indicators.note: to cover something is to go around it, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: a rap is a criminal charge, as in a murder rap
M is the abbreviation for mass in physics

explanation.surface: A fee that hides a large-scale fraud.
explanation.walkthrough: RA(M)P. Ramp is old British slang for a swindle or racket, especially one that pushes prices up.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a ramp is a racket or confidence trick, a dishonest scheme to extract money.

clue.text: Concerned about a youngster’s sanity

blocks.note: re means about or concerning, as in a letter heading
taken as written
a son is a young male child

explanation.surface: Someone worried about whether a child is mentally sound.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's reads as possessive but is 'is', linking wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To lose one's reason is to lose one's mind, so the word names soundness of mental faculties.

clue.text: Birth almost taking a month, but this shouldn’t end in tears

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
to take something in is to hold it inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: origin, a birth or beginning, without its last letter
taken as written
M is the abbreviation for month

explanation.surface: A pregnancy running almost a month over, which one hopes will not end in tears.
explanation.walkthrough: ORIG(A M)I. 'End in tears' reads as weeping, but tears here are rips in paper: a folded paper model should not get torn.
explanation.definitionFit: The Japanese art of folding paper into shapes ought not to involve rips, a cryptic pun on tears as rips.

clue.text: Buzzer didn’t make much noise?

blocks.note: first meaning: an insect that buzzes
second, split reading: was quiet, written as WAS plus P, the musical marking for piano

explanation.surface: A doorbell or buzzer that barely made a sound.
explanation.walkthrough: Buzzer suggests a doorbell, but it is a buzzing insect. P (piano) is the musical marking for quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: A stinging insect makes a buzzing sound in flight, so it is a playful description as a thing that buzzes.

clue.text: Two judges see a mess, after torturing outlaw

indicators.note: torturing twists and wrenches, so the letters are wrenched out of order

blocks.note: J is the abbreviation for judge, twice
taken as written

explanation.surface: Two judges view the aftermath of a brutal interrogation of a criminal.
explanation.walkthrough: The two Js join the other letters in the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: He was a notorious American bandit who robbed banks and trains in the nineteenth-century Wild West.

clue.text: As a precaution putting in last protein

indicators.note: the opening word of the phrase is moved to the end, so its front chunk goes to the back

blocks.note: in case, as in 'take an umbrella in case'

explanation.surface: Adding protein to a diet at the end, just to be safe.
explanation.walkthrough: IN CASE becomes CASE IN when the IN is shifted to the end; the IN in the indicator names the chunk to move.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the main protein found in milk and cheese, so a specific example of the general class.

clue.text: Singer’s strong emotion in costume

indicators.note: in places one thing inside another

blocks.note: heat as in the heat of passion or anger
wear means clothing, as in evening wear

explanation.surface: A vocalist pours feeling into the part while in costume.
explanation.walkthrough: W(HEAT)EAR. Singer suggests an opera performer, but crosswords often use it for a songbird.
explanation.definitionFit: This small songbird is a passerine, so it qualifies as a songster; birds are a common crossword sense.

clue.text: Do not apply for ring

blocks.note: 'do not apply' is rephrased as 'are not applicable', so the verb becomes ARE
N/A, the form abbreviation for not applicable

explanation.surface: A warning not to put in a bid for a wedding band or boxing bout.
explanation.walkthrough: Things that do not apply are N/A, so 'do not apply' becomes ARE N/A.
explanation.definitionFit: A boxing ring or circus ring is an enclosed space for performance or contest, the same as an arena.

clue.text: Bargain I secured in party

indicators.note: something secured in a place is held within it

blocks.note: taken as written
the Scottish National Party

explanation.surface: A politician boasting of a deal locked down inside the party.
explanation.walkthrough: SN(I)P. In British English a snip is something cheap, a real bargain.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal British usage calls an item going cheaply a snip, meaning a very good buy at a low price.

clue.text: Steps in dog mess clearly marked

indicators.note: a mess is disorder, so the letters are jumbled into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone treads in something a dog left that should have been flagged with a warning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dog mess' reads as one unpleasant noun phrase; mess is the signal and dog is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A route with guide posts and directions is made obvious to travellers, so it is plainly indicated.

clue.text: Fraud involving press ticket

indicators.note: to involve is to take in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a con is a swindle
Oxford University Press

explanation.surface: A scam involving tickets sold through the newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: C(OUP)ON. The press here is a publisher, Oxford University Press, not the newspapers.
explanation.definitionFit: A voucher entitling the holder to a discount or item is a kind of slip, much like a token or pass.

clue.text: A classical language has spread outside old German province

indicators.note: outside means wrapped around, so one piece surrounds the other

blocks.note: taken as written
the language of ancient Rome
pâté, a savoury spread

explanation.surface: A scholar notes that an ancient tongue once spread far beyond a German region.
explanation.walkthrough: P(A LATIN)ATE. Spread wants to be a verb, but it is a noun: pâté, something spread on toast.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rhenish territory ruled by a count palatine in the Holy Roman Empire was a historic German state.

clue.text: Yankee dropping in moving near jam pot

indicators.note: moving means shifting about, so the letters are rearranged
to drop in is to fall inside, so one letter is placed within the others

blocks.note: taken as written
Yankee is Y in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: An American wanders near a pot of jam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jam pot' reads as one thing, but pot is the definition: cannabis.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are slang for marijuana; the girl's name is an old pun on the Spanish word for cannabis.

clue.text: Memorial needs much slimming down for narrow inlet

indicators.note: slimming a word down a lot leaves just a small inner portion of it

blocks.note: trim the front and back, keeping only three inner letters

explanation.surface: A war memorial is costing too much and must be trimmed down.
explanation.walkthrough: Strip MEMO and L from MEMORIAL to leave RIA.
explanation.definitionFit: A ria is a long drowned river valley open to the sea, a narrow coastal water body.

clue.text: Excuse me: shut away poison

blocks.note: hem or ahem, the little cough used to get attention
to lock up is to shut away

explanation.surface: Someone politely interrupts to ask that the poison be locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: Hem is the throat-clearing noise people make instead of saying 'excuse me'.
explanation.definitionFit: The plant famously drunk by Socrates yields a toxic extract, so it names a classic deadly drug.

clue.text: Pretend not to see prune

blocks.note: first meaning: to snub, as in cutting someone dead
second meaning: to trim back

explanation.walkthrough: Prune looks like the dried plum, but it is the gardening verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Snubbing an acquaintance in the street is to cut them, and trimming a plant's branches is cutting too.

clue.text: David, say, has not succeeded as fortune-teller

indicators.note: lacking something means it is removed from the word

blocks.note: King David is traditionally the author of the Psalms
S is the abbreviation for succeeded in genealogies

explanation.surface: A man called David failed to make it as a fortune-teller.
explanation.walkthrough: PSALMIST minus S. David reads as any man's name, but it is the biblical king and psalm writer.
explanation.definitionFit: A reader of the lines on people's hands claims to predict their future, a type of clairvoyant.

clue.text: Hairy bit of damage in small place I look after

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small
PL is the abbreviation for place
taken as written
to tend is to look after

explanation.surface: Someone surveys a nasty patch of damage in a small house they care for.
explanation.walkthrough: Hairy reads as alarming, as in a hairy moment, but it is literal: damage to a hair.
explanation.definitionFit: When the tip of a strand of hair frays into two, that frayed tip is damage to one's hair.

clue.text: Scuffle that is a problem for flock

blocks.note: a scrap is a fight
i.e., Latin id est, that is

explanation.surface: A fight breaks out, which troubles a church congregation.
explanation.walkthrough: Flock suggests a church congregation, but it is literal sheep.
explanation.definitionFit: This fatal brain disease affects sheep and goats, so it is a serious health issue for any shepherd's animals.

clue.text: Extremely happy in financial district, not going anywhere

blocks.note: EC is the postcode for the City of London, its financial centre
static means not moving

explanation.surface: A banker is delighted in the City, with no plans to move.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like it places one piece inside another, but it is just a link; the pieces sit side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Both describe overwhelming joy or delight, the state of being thrilled beyond ordinary pleasure.

clue.text: Butcher has no time to train darling child

indicators.note: lacking something means it is removed from the word
to train is to shape or bend into a new form, so the letters are reshaped

blocks.note: taken as written
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A butcher too busy to coach a beloved child.
explanation.walkthrough: BUTCHER loses T to leave BUCHER, which is then rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweet, innocent-looking little one is often called an angel, and this word for a winged angel is used affectionately.

clue.text: Rock band’s half season

indicators.note: half of a word keeps only one portion of its letters

blocks.note: the front two of its four letters
to season food is to salt it

explanation.surface: A rock group only plays for half the season.
explanation.walkthrough: Rock band reads as one phrase, but Rock is the definition and season is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a dark volcanic stone formed from cooled lava, so it is a specific kind of mineral formation.

clue.text: No good cycling on island, not much cover

indicators.note: no means without, so a letter is taken away

blocks.note: biking is cycling
G is the abbreviation for good
I is the abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: Cycling round an island is no fun when there is little shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: BIKING loses G, then the island letter goes on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A two-piece swimsuit reveals a great deal of skin, so the garment covers very little of the body.

clue.text: Stamp coin on reverse, incising line

indicators.note: to incise is to cut into, so one piece is set inside the other

blocks.note: a penny is a coin
the reverse of something is its back
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: Instructions for minting: stamp the coin's reverse, cutting a line into it.
explanation.walkthrough: Stamp looks like a minting verb, and reverse like a coin's tails side, but Stamp is the definition and reverse simply means back.
explanation.definitionFit: Issued in Britain in 1840, it was the world's first adhesive postage stamp, so a famous philatelic example.

clue.text: In speech, Oxbridge representative breathed hard

indicators.note: in speech means as heard spoken, so a word with the same sound is wanted

blocks.note: a Blue is a sportsperson who has represented Oxford or Cambridge

explanation.surface: An Oxford or Cambridge athlete is panting while talking.
explanation.walkthrough: At Oxford and Cambridge, competing against the other university earns a Blue, named after the team colours.
explanation.definitionFit: To puff or exhale forcefully, as after running, is the past tense of the verb meaning to expel air.

clue.text: Scottish island? Objection: English

blocks.note: a but is an objection, as in no ifs or buts
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A quiz answer about a Scottish isle is challenged as being English.
explanation.walkthrough: Bute is an island in the Firth of Clyde, off western Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an isle in the Firth of Clyde, so it is one example of the many islands of Scotland.

clue.text: Difficulty over bit of ribbon that may stick to one’s coat

definitions.text: that may stick to one’s coat

indicators.note: in a down clue over means turned upside down, so the letters run backwards
a bit of a word is a single letter, here its opening one

blocks.note: the rub is the difficulty, as in 'there's the rub'
its opening letter

explanation.surface: A snag over a scrap of ribbon caught on someone's coat.
explanation.walkthrough: A burr is a prickly seed head that clings to clothing and animal fur.
explanation.definitionFit: Prickly seed cases hook onto fabric and fur as you brush past plants, so they cling to clothing.

clue.text: Join together, but it turns loose

indicators.note: the word it is spun round on the spot, so those two letters run the other way

blocks.note: to unite is to join together

explanation.surface: A paradox: something meant to bind ends up coming apart.
explanation.walkthrough: In UNITE, the IT flips to TI. Loose is a verb here, meaning to set free.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to loose means to release or unfasten, the same as undoing a knot or bond.

clue.text: Ill-educated, go in for rambling tirade

indicators.note: rambling means wandering aimlessly, so the letters wander out of order

blocks.note: taken as written
a rant is an angry tirade

explanation.surface: An uneducated person launches into a long, wandering rant.
explanation.walkthrough: Rambling sits beside tirade as if describing it, but it shuffles the earlier words.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking knowledge or schooling makes a person unknowing, so the adjectives are close synonyms.
